claim: Make the prompt input the dominant above-the-fold element on an AI product's entry screen — size it large enough to read as the primary action, and let the rest of the page recede around it.
why: An oversized input invites immediate use, so the user experiences the product instead of reading claims about it; it also yields a spare, single-focus composition that scans instantly.
when: The core value of the product is delivered through a text prompt and can be demonstrated in one interaction.
fails: Products where a first prompt cannot produce useful output without setup, connected data, or account state — there the empty box reads as a demand rather than an invitation.

claim: For prompt-first tools, consider skipping the marketing landing page entirely and routing arrivals straight into the working interface.
why: The interface is the strongest possible demonstration; leading products have removed the intermediate page because the trial itself converts better than the pitch.
when: The product is self-explanatory at first contact and can run at least one meaningful interaction before signup.
fails: When the product needs positioning, pricing context, or trust-building before use — an unexplained interface leaves an unconvinced visitor nothing to read.

claim: Render attached files as visual preview tiles inside the input — thumbnail for images, page or document card for PDFs — instead of a filename string.
why: A preview confirms the right file was attached before the user commits the prompt, closing the loop on an otherwise blind action.
when: Any input that accepts file or image attachments.

claim: Collapse large pasted content into a compact, labelled, expandable block on paste rather than letting it expand the input to full height.
why: Bulk text like code otherwise dominates the composer and the conversation, pushing controls and prior context off screen; a collapsed block preserves the content while keeping the layout stable.
when: Inputs that regularly receive multi-line pastes — code, logs, spreadsheets, long documents.
fails: Short pastes the user still wants to edit inline — collapsing those adds a click to a trivial edit.

claim: When the tool serves many distinct jobs, expose mode selection as chips directly on the input (e.g. brainstorm, analyse, draft) instead of burying it in settings.
why: Naming the mode at the point of writing steers the model and simultaneously teaches the user what the tool can do, without requiring them to phrase intent perfectly.
when: General-purpose AI tools whose output quality varies sharply by task type.
fails: Single-purpose tools, where mode chips add decisions to a flow that has only one correct mode.

claim: Let users attach explicit context references to a prompt and display those references as persistent pills above or inside the input.
why: Visible context is a pre-submission contract: the user can see what the system will look at and correct it before spending a turn, which removes the guesswork about whether the model has what it needs.
when: Tools operating over a user's own corpus — files, codebases, documents, records.

claim: Offer source connections (cloud drives, repositories, design files, internal systems) as buttons on the composer itself, at the moment context is being assembled.
why: Integrations placed in the composer are discovered and used in the flow where they matter, rather than being lost in an account settings page.
when: Products whose answers improve materially with access to the user's external systems.

claim: Apply progressive disclosure inside the input: keep the default state to a text field and a send affordance, and put power controls behind a single toggle such as an advanced mode switch.
why: A minimal default keeps the first-run experience unintimidating while still giving experienced users a short path to depth.
when: Inputs that have accumulated more than a handful of options.

claim: Surface cost or consumption signals — such as an estimated token or credit cost — adjacent to the input before submission.
why: Showing the price of an action before it is taken lets the user adjust scope rather than discover the cost afterwards.
when: Metered products where prompt length or mode materially changes what the user is charged.
fails: Flat-rate or unmetered products, where a cost readout only introduces anxiety about a number the user cannot act on.

claim: Fill the pre-response wait with a small, seamlessly looping, continuously moving indicator — bouncing dots or a slow rotating mark — rather than a progress bar or static spinner freeze.
why: Generation has no knowable completion percentage, so a looping animation honestly signals 'working' while fluid motion makes the same wall-clock delay feel shorter.
when: Any indeterminate wait between prompt submission and first token.
fails: Long multi-step operations where the user needs to know which stage is running — there a staged status line beats an abstract loop.

claim: Treat the composer as the product's control panel: every capability the user needs before sending — attachments, context, mode, integrations, settings, cost — should be reachable from it without navigating away.
why: Consolidating pre-send controls at the single point of intent means the user never has to leave the thought they are writing to configure the system.
when: Conversational or prompt-driven interfaces generally.
fails: Overloading the composer past the point of legibility; the consolidation only works when paired with disclosure so the resting state stays simple.

claim: Design each composer affordance to answer 'does the system have what it needs?' before submission, not after.
why: Every element named — file previews, context pills, mode chips, cost estimates — is a pre-flight confirmation; the shared purpose is converting a blind submit into a checked one.
when: Any interface where a submitted action is slow, metered, or hard to undo.

claim: Any product that generates text, code, or images must persist past generations in a browsable history surface rather than letting output disappear when the view changes.
why: Generated output is expensive to reproduce and users routinely need to return to an earlier result; discarding it forces regeneration and destroys trust in the tool as a place to work.
when: The product produces artifacts the user might reference, compare, or reuse later.
fails: For ephemeral, low-value interactions like autocomplete suggestions or inline rewrites, where a history entry per generation creates noise instead of value.

claim: Choose the history's organizing axis by how users will look things up: use a chronological session list when generations are standalone conversations, and anchor generations to their source object when they modify an existing document or block.
why: Retrieval succeeds when the index matches the user's mental model of where the output came from; a flat time list is useless for finding the third rewrite of one paragraph, and per-block anchoring is useless for recalling last week's open-ended chat.
when: Deciding the information architecture of the history panel at the start of the design.
fails: Products with both modes may need both axes — forcing one structure on a mixed workflow hides half the history.

claim: Render each history entry with a preview of its first line or a short content snippet rather than a title, timestamp, or generic label alone.
why: Users recognize their own output by its content; a list of identically-shaped rows forces them to open each one to identify it, which is scanning by brute force.
when: Designing the list-item template for any history or run log.
fails: When outputs are images or non-textual artifacts, where a thumbnail replaces the text snippet as the recognition cue.

claim: Ship search over history in the first version, not as a later addition, and treat it as the affordance that justifies retention at all.
why: Without search, an accumulating list gets worse as it grows — volume becomes a liability instead of an asset, so the archive turns into storage no one opens.
when: History can grow past what one screen shows, which is nearly always.

claim: Give users deletion of individual history entries alongside search and previews.
why: Retrievability requires the user to control what is in the pile; without pruning, irrelevant or unwanted generations dilute search results and users lose the ability to keep the space meaningful.
when: History persists across sessions.
fails: Where audit or compliance requirements mandate retention, deletion must be scoped to hiding from the user's view rather than true erasure.

claim: Treat generation history and persistent memory as two distinct surfaces: history is an append-only log of every output, memory is a curated set of facts that shape future behaviour.
why: They answer different questions and need different interactions — you scan history to find one past thing, but you audit memory to understand why the system is behaving as it does.
when: The product both stores past outputs and carries state forward into new generations.

claim: If the system retains persistent memory about a user, expose that memory in a dedicated, reachable panel in the main product surface instead of burying it in a settings sub-page.
why: Memory silently alters every future output; when it is invisible, users cannot explain unexpected behaviour or correct a wrong fact, and the system feels unpredictable rather than personalized.
when: Any AI feature that carries facts about the user forward between sessions.

claim: Build the memory panel with three controls: a view of how much memory is stored and how much room remains, bulk selection and deletion of stale entries, and a direct way to add a fact the user wants remembered.
why: Read-only visibility only shows the problem; users need to correct and curate what the system knows, and one-at-a-time deletion makes clearing accumulated cruft impractical.
when: Implementing a user-facing memory surface.

claim: Show a concrete storage or capacity indicator on the memory panel so users understand memory as a finite, managed resource.
why: A visible limit motivates curation and sets the expectation that not everything can be retained, which makes eventual forgetting feel like a rule rather than a bug.
when: Memory has real capacity limits or a retention policy.
fails: If capacity is effectively unbounded, a meter invents scarcity and creates anxiety with no corresponding action for the user to take.

claim: Let users select a span inside an AI-generated response and issue an edit instruction scoped to that span, instead of forcing them back to the main prompt box to re-ask for the whole output.
why: The selection itself carries the context, so the instruction can be short and the rest of the output is left untouched — that is the friction being removed.
when: Any surface where the AI emits a block of editable text the user is likely to want to adjust partially: chat answers, drafts, generated copy, documents.
fails: Outputs that aren't decomposable — a single number, a chart, a code file where a local edit breaks global consistency — where a scoped rewrite produces an internally inconsistent result.

claim: Keep the inline edit control compact — a small floating bar or menu anchored to the selection, not a panel that covers the text being edited.
why: The user needs to keep reading the surrounding text to judge the edit; a large surface hides the very context that makes the interaction contextual.
when: Designing the affordance that appears on text selection or on hover over a generated block.
fails: The edit genuinely requires structured input (multiple fields, tone sliders, file attachment) — then escalate to a side panel rather than cramming it inline.

claim: Pair a small set of preset actions (rephrase, improve, fix spelling, shorten) with a free-text field, rather than shipping only one or the other.
why: Presets cover the common 80% in one click and teach the user what the surface can do; the free-text field catches everything else without needing a longer menu.
when: Building the inline edit menu for generated or user-written prose.
fails: Preset lists grow past roughly half a dozen items and the menu stops being scannable — at that point the presets are doing the free-text field's job badly.

claim: Bind the inline edit trigger to a keyboard shortcut so power users never leave the keyboard to revise.
why: The pattern's value is speed; requiring a mouse trip to a hover menu reintroduces the friction the pattern exists to remove.
when: Writing-heavy tools where users are already typing when they decide to revise.
fails: Touch-first or mobile surfaces with no keyboard, where selection handles and a contextual toolbar are the only viable trigger.

claim: Apply the edit as a diff to the selected span, leaving everything outside the selection byte-identical, so the interaction reads as revision rather than regeneration.
why: If the surrounding text visibly shifts or rewords, the user loses trust that they are in control of the document and reverts to reviewing the whole output every time.
when: Any scoped AI edit inside a larger body of content.
fails: The requested change has necessary knock-on effects elsewhere (renaming a subject, changing tense throughout) — then surface the wider diff explicitly rather than silently editing outside the selection.

claim: Anchor the edit affordance to the unit the user thinks in — per-paragraph controls for structured documents, per-selection controls for freeform prose.
why: Two shipped variants of the same pattern differ exactly here, and each matches its host's content model: block-based docs get block-level buttons, continuous prose gets selection-level ones.
when: Deciding where the inline AI controls attach in a given editor.

claim: Show scoped edits landing in place with no loading state that blanks the surrounding content, so the result reads as real-time.
why: A full-output spinner communicates 'I am regenerating everything', which is the mental model the pattern is trying to replace.
when: Rendering the response to an inline edit request.

claim: For any AI feature that retrieves before it answers, render the retrieval process as visible UI — a list of steps the system took — rather than only the final answer.
why: Users cannot audit a model's internals, so process visibility is the only available proxy for trustworthiness; showing sourced work moves the output from 'asserted' to 'evidenced'.
when: The system does grounded or multi-step work — search, RAG, tool calls, agentic chains — where real intermediate artifacts exist to show.
fails: The model answers purely from parametric knowledge; fabricating a reasoning trail for a single-shot completion is theatre and will mislead users about how the answer was produced.

claim: Structure the reasoning trail as three to five discrete, named steps that each describe an action in verb-first form ('Searching docs', 'Extracting quotes', 'Drafting answer') rather than a status noun ('Step 2', 'Processing').
why: Verb-first labels tell the user what is happening right now, which converts dead time into narrated progress; a small fixed count keeps the sequence scannable and implies a bounded end.
when: Designing the step list for a research, agent, or multi-stage generation component.
fails: The real pipeline has a variable or very large number of stages — then group into phases rather than exposing every internal call, or the trail becomes a log dump.

claim: Reveal steps sequentially with a staggered fade-in — each step appears only as its stage begins — instead of rendering the full list up front with pending states.
why: Sequential reveal makes the passage of time legible and gives the impression of live work; a fully rendered list of greyed-out future steps reads as a static checklist and gives away that the timing is scripted.
when: The stages complete at roughly human-perceptible intervals during a wait of a few seconds or more.
fails: Steps resolve near-instantly — a rapid cascade of appearing rows reads as flicker; and if users need to know the total scope of work ahead, hiding future steps removes that information.

claim: Within the trail, surface the concrete evidence objects — document titles, source links, quoted excerpts — not just the abstract stage names.
why: Named, clickable artifacts are verifiable; a step label alone is an unverifiable claim that work occurred, which buys perceived intelligence without earning it.
when: The retrieval layer returns identifiable sources that can be attributed and linked.
fails: Sources are confidential, unstable, or too numerous to render inline — then summarize counts and offer a drill-in rather than dumping every reference.

claim: Design the reasoning trail to double as the loading state for the answer, so the wait is filled with substantive content instead of an indeterminate spinner.
why: The trail has to occupy the same interval the user would otherwise spend staring at a progress indicator; giving that interval informational payload makes the same latency feel shorter and more purposeful.
when: Generation takes long enough that a bare loading indicator would otherwise be required.
fails: Latency is short enough that the trail would flash and vanish before it can be read.

claim: Show the logical dependency between steps — that a later step consumed the output of an earlier one — rather than presenting the stages as unrelated parallel tasks.
why: A visible chain communicates that the system reasoned across hops, which is the specific quality that reads as intelligence; a flat set of ticked boxes reads as mere task completion.
when: The underlying pipeline genuinely passes intermediate results forward, such as retrieval feeding extraction feeding synthesis.

claim: Never let an AI action produce a static screen — emit visible partial progress within the first moment of the wait, because the failure users react to is absence of feedback, not duration itself.
why: Perceived wait time is driven by uncertainty; a screen that is visibly doing something reads as shorter and more trustworthy than an identical wait with no signal.
when: Any operation with non-trivial or unpredictable latency: model inference, generation, long fetches.
fails: Sub-300ms operations, where a flashed loading state creates more visual noise than the wait it covers.

claim: Stream text output token-by-token or word-by-word as it arrives instead of buffering the full response and revealing it at once.
why: Incremental arrival gives the user something to read immediately and reframes the remaining wait as anticipation of what comes next rather than dead time.
when: Language-model responses rendered as prose in a chat or answer surface.
fails: Outputs that must be validated, parsed, or reformatted before they are safe or coherent to show — structured data, code that gets post-processed, or answers subject to a moderation pass.

claim: For non-text output, render a skeleton of the result's actual layout — placeholder blocks matching the shape and position of the images and text that are coming — rather than a generic spinner.
why: A structural placeholder communicates what is being built, not just that something is happening, so the interface reads as alive and already partly formed.
when: Generating composite output with known structure: canvases, wireframes, cards, dashboards, feeds.
fails: The output's shape is unknown ahead of time, where a wrong skeleton misleads the user about what they will get.

claim: Size and position each placeholder to match the real content, so finished output drops into the space already reserved and nothing reflows.
why: Reusing the same geometry for the loading and loaded states removes layout shift and makes completion feel like a resolution of the placeholder rather than a page replacement.
when: Any skeleton-to-content transition.
fails: Content with genuinely variable dimensions, where an approximate skeleton still beats a spinner but some shift is unavoidable.

claim: Animate the placeholder with a continuous shimmer or pulse rather than leaving it as a flat grey block.
why: Motion is what separates 'loading' from 'broken' — a static grey rectangle is indistinguishable from a failed render.
when: Every skeleton state.
fails: Long multi-minute jobs, where an endless shimmer with no progress signal stops reassuring and starts looking hung; pair it with staged status text.

claim: Anchor the loading indicator in the exact location the result will occupy, not in a modal, overlay, or global top-of-page bar.
why: In-place feedback ties the wait to the specific thing being produced and preserves the user's spatial context.
when: Component-level generation inside a larger interface.
fails: Blocking operations that genuinely invalidate the whole view, which warrant a global state.

claim: Treat the loading state as a designed screen with its own composition, not as a fallback — give it the same typographic and spacing treatment as the loaded state.
why: Users spend real time in this state during AI work, so it carries as much of the product's perceived quality as the finished output.
when: Products where generation is a core, frequent interaction.

claim: Attach a confidence indicator to every AI-generated answer, not only to the ones the model rates as weak.
why: If the indicator only appears when confidence is low, its absence becomes ambiguous — users cannot tell a confident answer from an unmeasured one, so the signal carries no information.
when: Any interface that presents probabilistic model output as a discrete answer users will act on.
fails: Outputs that are deterministic or retrieved verbatim from a source of record, where a confidence score is meaningless theatre.

claim: Render the confidence signal as a plain-language label first ('high confidence', 'unverified'), and keep the raw percentage behind a click.
why: Most users cannot calibrate what 61% means, but they can act on 'unverified'; the number still matters to the minority who want to audit, so hide it rather than delete it.
when: Consumer-facing or mixed-audience AI surfaces where the score comes from a model that emits real probabilities.
fails: Expert tooling and evaluation dashboards, where practitioners want the number inline and a word-label is a lossy downgrade.

claim: Place the confidence element immediately below the response block it describes, scoped to that single output.
why: Confidence is a property of one specific answer; a global or header-level indicator would imply the whole session or model is uniformly reliable.
when: Response streams where multiple generated answers stack in one view.

claim: Use a pill-shaped bar as the container — small, horizontal, visually subordinate to the answer text.
why: The indicator is metadata; giving it a large or heavy treatment competes with the content the user actually came for, while a pill still reads as a discrete, tappable object.
when: Confidence metadata sitting under body-weight response text.
fails: When confidence is the primary decision axis (e.g. a triage queue sorted by certainty), where it should be promoted to a primary column or chart.

claim: Define a discrete band scale mapping numeric confidence to labels, and give the lowest band its own explicit flag rather than a quiet low number.
why: A displayed 61% still looks like a positive assertion; an 'uncertain' or 'unverified' badge forces the user to register that the system is not vouching for the answer.
when: Model returns a continuous score you must translate into UI states.
fails: Poorly calibrated models where the score does not track actual accuracy — banding then launders noise into an authoritative-looking label.

claim: Make the confidence pill interactive so the numeric value is one tap away, rather than shipping it as a static badge.
why: Progressive disclosure keeps the default view calm while preserving an audit path for users who need to justify trusting or discarding the output.
when: Any confidence indicator using a summarised label.
